1-a.question: How are **all the data** for all subjects, sessions, and trials loaded in?
1-a.decision_correctness_justification: The AI loads only 12 of the 44 ephys sessions the paper reports (3,116 trials / 518 units vs the reference's 13,762 trials / 1,954 units), restricting itself to the two-context cohort loaded by Figure8a_thru_c.m and reading only /app/data/Ephys_Behavior. The rationale is real and paper-grounded: the paper states 'In 12 sessions from six mice, animals performed the two-context task... 522 units', and the decoder must predict WC vs DR context, which only that cohort exhibits; the AI's 518 units is a strong match to the paper's 522. But the justification is overstated in one respect I checked against the raw files: the claim that the other 13 fixed-delay sessions have no 'genuine alternating WC blocks' is only partly true (JEB13_2022-09-14 has 48 autowater trials in blocks of up to 22, JEB15_2022-07-28 has 45 in blocks of 22/7/7/9, JEB14_2022-08-25 has 55), and five of the excluded RD sessions also have autowater trials. Five of the six decoder outputs (lick, outcome, tongue, paw, motion) need no WC context at all, so ~77% of the available trials and ~73% of the units were discarded for a constraint that binds only one output. The exclusion also conveniently coincides with a capability gap: no v5 MAT reader is implemented, so the 11 v5 files in RandomizedDelay_Ephys_Behavior could not have been read. Defensible and well documented, but the scale of the data loss should be checked by a human.
1-a.code_correctness_justification: The hard-coded SESSIONS list matches the 12 sessions and probes named in the authors' two-context script; h5py reads only the needed obj fields and scipy.io reads the v5 motion-energy files. The full run log shows all 12 sessions loaded without error, and the converted pickle contains exactly those 12 sessions with the stated native trial counts (3,626) — the code implements the cohort it describes.

1-b.question: How are the data split into subjects (mice)?
1-b.decision_correctness_justification: Same rule as the reference: the animal is the token before the underscore in the session name (equivalently the first element of the session tuple), carried through to `subjects` and `subject_idx`. The AI keeps 7 distinct IDs (JEB6, JEB7, EKH1, EKH3, JGR2, JGR3, JEB19) and explicitly documents that the paper reports six mice for this cohort rather than silently merging IDs — the same honest handling the reference applies. The count differs from the reference's 14 only because of the cohort decision graded in 1-a.
1-b.code_correctness_justification: `subjects` is built in first-appearance order and `subject_idx = [subjects.index(animal) ...]` has one entry per session; the verification log shows 7 subjects with the correct session counts per subject (JEB19: 4, JEB7: 2, JGR2: 2, rest 1).

1-c.question: How are the data split into sessions?
1-c.decision_correctness_justification: One data_structure_*.mat file = one session = one element of neural/input/output/brain_region_idx, with the probe(s) taken from the authors' load<ANM>_ALMVideo.m loaders and multi-probe support for concatenation, exactly as in the reference. All session-scoped quantities (video clock offset, the three discretisation thresholds, the unit set) are computed inside the session, which is correct. The only difference from the reference is which sessions enter, already graded in 1-a.
1-c.code_correctness_justification: `process_session` is called once per tuple and its outputs are appended as one session each; the probe filter `if probe_index not in probes: continue` implements the loader-specified probe selection. Verification reports 12 sessions with per-session neuron counts 27-67.

1-d.question: How are the data split into trials?
1-d.decision_correctness_justification: Identical to the reference: a trial is one row of the Bpod table defined by obj.bp.Ntrials, with one goCue per trial, spikes carrying their 1-based trial index and camera frames/motion-energy traces stored per trial, so no trial boundaries need reconstructing. The AI goes slightly further than the reference by asserting every per-trial array has exactly Ntrials entries rather than truncating, which is a reasonable safety check for this cohort (the reference truncates because some fields are longer in sessions the AI does not load).
1-d.code_correctness_justification: Each bp field is read, raveled and length-checked against Ntrials with an explicit raise; the full conversion ran without raising, and the native trial counts printed per session match the raw files (verified independently: 382, 346, 254, 305, 426, 267, 254, 261, 276, 324, 230, 301).

1-e.question: How are trials filtered based on quality controls?
1-e.decision_correctness_justification: The AI drops early-lick and photostimulation trials, exactly the reference's two paper-based filters ('Trials in which the animal contacted the lickport before the reward were omitted from analyses'; every params.condition contains ~stim.enable), and keeps ignore trials because the decoder spec requires an 'ignore' class — the same reasoning the reference gives. It adds finite-goCue and one-hot flag consistency requirements; I verified these drop zero additional trials, so retention is identical to the reference rule (3,116 of 3,626). The reference's extra cut for trials past the end of the recording is absent, but I verified no such trials exist in these 12 sessions (max spiking trial == Ntrials in all 12), so the omission has no effect here — it would matter only if the cohort were expanded.
1-e.code_correctness_justification: The single `retained = np.flatnonzero(~early & ~stim & isfinite(go) & (outcome_sum==1) & (side_sum==1))` implements exactly the described rule, and all downstream arrays are indexed by `retained`; I reproduced the retained counts per session from the raw files and they match the conversion log exactly.

2-a.question: What variables in the raw data is the `neural` data derived from?
2-a.decision_correctness_justification: Same source variables as the reference: obj.clu{probe}.trial, .trialtm and .quality for the loader-specified probe(s), with bp.ev.goCue supplying the alignment and bp.Ntrials the trial axis. Waveforms and absolute spike times are correctly ignored.
2-a.code_correctness_justification: load_neural dereferences exactly those HDF5 datasets per cluster and asserts trial/trialtm length agreement. I independently re-derived session 0 / unit 0 from the raw file and reproduced the stored 500-bin trace to 5e-6 (float32 rounding), confirming the stated sources and indexing.

2-b.question: How is the `neural` data processed?
2-b.decision_correctness_justification: Counts are converted to spikes/s and smoothed with the reference's own causal half-Gaussian (mySmooth's gausswin(15) with the first half zeroed, renormalised, using its idiosyncratic 'reflect' padding of the first 15 samples followed by trimming). This is a more faithful reproduction of getSeq.m/mySmooth.m than the reference solution's symmetric 14 ms Gaussian, and a causal kernel is also the safer choice for a decoder because it cannot leak future activity backwards in time. Like the reference, no normalisation, baseline subtraction or z-scoring is applied and rates are stored as float32.
2-b.code_correctness_justification: The sliding-window/einsum convolution is equivalent to conv(...,'same') (the AI verified it against np.convolve to 2e-16), and the prefix-pad/trim reproduces mySmooth. One small deviation from the stated 'Match MATLAB gausswin(N)': the kernel uses exp(-0.5*(alpha*x/(N/2))^2) whereas MATLAB's gausswin uses (N-1)/2, making the kernel ~7% wider (sigma 3.0 vs 2.8 bins). I confirmed the stored data matches the AI's own formula to 5e-6 and that switching to the true MATLAB denominator changes values by up to ~4 Hz on a 4 Hz unit — a smoothing-width difference, not an alignment or scaling error, so the implementation still realises the decision as documented in the notes.

2-c.question: How is the `neural` data filtered based on quality controls?
2-c.decision_correctness_justification: Two filters, the same two as the reference: the manual curation label and a mean-rate cut. The AI's drop set {garbage, gabrga, noisy, real?} is exactly findClusters.m's quality='all' list (the reference additionally drops 'poor', a deviation the AI does not make), matching case-insensitively as the reference does, and keeping multi-units and unlabelled clusters. The >1 Hz cut matches the paper ('All units with firing rates exceeding 1 Hz were included in all other analyses') and params.lowFR = 1 in every figure script. The resulting 518 units against the paper's stated 522 for this cohort is a genuine, well-executed sanity check, and the AI explicitly refused to tune the threshold to force agreement.
2-c.code_correctness_justification: The quality string is read, stripped, lower-cased and tested against BAD_QUALITIES, and units are appended only when `mean_rate > 1.0`. Verification reports 518 ALM neurons with per-session counts 27-67. Minor note: the mean rate is taken over all native trials (including the ~14% later dropped) and over smoothed rates, whereas removeLowFRClusters.m averages condition PSTHs; this is a defensible approximation and does not contradict the stated decision.

2-d.question: How is the per-trial `neural` data aligned to the event described in the `instructions`?
2-d.decision_correctness_justification: Identical to the reference and to alignSpikes.m: trialtm minus the goCue of the spike's own trial, both already on the behaviour clock, with no offset or interpolation; spikes outside the window simply fall off the histogram edges. The metadata correctly records that for WC trials the same field is the water-presentation time.
2-d.code_correctness_justification: `aligned = trial_times[valid] - go[trials-1]` with 1-based to 0-based conversion, followed by searchsorted into EDGES. My independent recomputation from the raw HDF5 reproduced the stored trace exactly, which would not happen under an alignment or off-by-one error.

2-e.question: What is the temporal resolution (time bin size) of the converted data? Is any temporal rebinning applied?
2-e.decision_correctness_justification: 10 ms bins over [-2.5, 2.5) = 500 bins, versus the reference's 5 ms / 1000 bins. Both values appear in the reference code; 10 ms (params.dt = 1/100) is in fact the setting used by nearly every analysis script in /app/code, including the two-context Figure 8 and the choice/context decoding pipelines, while 1/200 appears only in getDefaultParams.m and three scripts. Spikes are binned directly at 10 ms (no rebinning of a finer grid) and the identical axis is shared by the input and the three video outputs. The window matches the reference's [-2.5, 2.5]; the AI explicitly considered and rejected Figure 8's [-3, 2.5]. Halving the temporal resolution relative to the expert is a real but well-argued difference.
2-e.code_correctness_justification: TIME/EDGES are module-level constants derived from DT=0.010; every stored array is (·, 500), metadata['time_bin_size']=10.0 ms and off_start/off_end are -2.5/2.5. Verification confirms T = 500 for all trials and input range [-2.5, 2.5].

3-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `input` *Time from go cue onset in seconds* derived from?
3-a.decision_correctness_justification: Same as the reference: the input is not a raw variable but the bin-centre time axis of the go-cue-aligned window, identical on every trial, which satisfies the spec's 'time from go cue onset in seconds (continuous, time-varying)'.
3-a.code_correctness_justification: `time_input = TIME.astype(np.float32)[None, :]` is copied into every trial; the stored values run -2.495 ... 2.495 as expected, and the AI's independent check matched all 3,116 trials to 2e-7.

3-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `input` *Time from go cue onset in seconds*?
3-b.decision_correctness_justification: None beyond constructing the axis, exactly as in the reference (bin centres = edges + dt/2, matching obj.time in getSeq.m). Nothing is normalised or rescaled.
3-b.code_correctness_justification: A single `np.arange(TMIN, TMAX, DT) + DT/2` cast to float32; I confirmed the first and last stored values are -2.495 and 2.495.

3-c.question: How is the `input` *Time from go cue onset in seconds* aligned with the neural data?
3-c.decision_correctness_justification: The input is the centre of the very bins the spikes are counted into, so bin k is the same interval in both streams by construction — the same argument the reference gives. The video streams are interpolated onto those same centres, so all five streams share one axis.
3-c.code_correctness_justification: EDGES and TIME are derived from the same TMIN/DT constants and used for the spike histogram and the input respectively; the --show-processing plots place the go cue at t=0 on both the neural raster and the behavioural traces.

4-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `output` *Lick direction* derived from?
4-a.decision_correctness_justification: Same variables as the reference: the instructed/rewarded side (bp.R, bp.L) combined with the outcome flags (bp.hit, bp.miss, bp.no), because the licked side itself is not recorded. The AI reads bp.no explicitly where the reference infers it; equivalent given the flags are one-hot (which the AI verifies).
4-a.code_correctness_justification: trial_labels reads exactly those five flags. The AI's independent check re-derived lick direction from the raw Bpod arrays for 36 trials across all 12 sessions and matched.

4-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `output` *Lick direction*?
4-b.decision_correctness_justification: Identical mapping to the reference: hit -> instructed side, miss -> opposite side, no-response -> a third 'none' class, with codes left=0, right=1, none=2 in the order the spec lists them, broadcast across all 500 bins so all six outputs share one array. The resulting 0.398/0.377/0.225 distribution is sensible.
4-b.code_correctness_justification: The if/elif/else in trial_labels implements exactly that mapping and the value is assigned to output[0] across all bins; verification reports lick direction values {left 0.398, right 0.377, none 0.225} with range [0, 2].

5-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `output` *Behavioral context* derived from?
5-a.decision_correctness_justification: bp.autowater, the same single flag the reference uses and the one the authors' condition expressions use to separate WC from DR.
5-a.code_correctness_justification: `autowater` is read into the bp dict as a boolean and used directly; the AI audited one session's block structure against the raw flag (first WC trial, seven transitions) and matched.

5-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `output` *Behavioral context*?
5-b.decision_correctness_justification: Direct relabelling autowater -> WC = 0, else DR = 1, matching the reference and the spec's (WC, DR) ordering, broadcast over time. Both classes are present in all 12 sessions (WC fraction 0.226-0.391), which is the property the AI's cohort choice was made to guarantee.
5-b.code_correctness_justification: `context = 0 if bool(bp['autowater'][trial]) else 1`, assigned to output[1]; verification shows {WC 0.315, DR 0.685} with per-session ranges [0, 1].

6-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `output` *Outcome* derived from?
6-a.decision_correctness_justification: bp.hit / bp.miss / bp.no — the same flags as the reference, which derives 'ignore' as the complement instead of reading bp.no. The AI additionally enforces that exactly one of the three is set on every retained trial, which validates the equivalence.
6-a.code_correctness_justification: All three flags are read and the one-hot condition is part of the retention mask; the conversion ran with no trials failing that test, and the independent 36-trial check matched outcomes.

6-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `output` *Outcome*?
6-b.decision_correctness_justification: Same three-way relabelling as the reference — miss -> incorrect (0), hit -> correct (1), otherwise ignore (2) — in the order the spec lists, broadcast over time, with ignore trials kept rather than dropped as the paper does. Distribution 0.106/0.669/0.225 is plausible for this task.
6-b.code_correctness_justification: `outcome = 1 if hit else (0 if miss else 2)` assigned to output[2]; verification reports {incorrect 0.106, correct 0.669, ignore 0.225}, and the ignore fraction equals the 'none' lick fraction as it must.

7-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `output` *Tongue velocity* derived from?
7-a.decision_correctness_justification: The AI uses only the side camera's 'tongue' feature (obj.traj{1}.ts x/y + frameTimes), whereas the reference fuses the side 'tongue' and bottom 'top_tongue' views after per-view normalisation. Using one view per feature is what the reference MATLAB code itself does (params.traj_features treats each view's features separately, and getKinematicsFromVideo never fuses views), so the choice is well grounded; the cost is a lower recovered visibility (91.9% 'not visible' bins vs the reference's ~88%), i.e. some licks seen only by the bottom camera are missed. Equally justifiable rather than better or worse. The AI correctly relies on x/y being NaN for untracked frames — I verified this is exactly equivalent to DeepLabCut likelihood <= 0.9 in these files, so the reference's explicit likelihood cut is reproduced implicitly.
7-a.code_correctness_justification: The side view's featNames are resolved, 'tongue' is located by name (raising if absent), and its x/y columns of ts are read for each trial together with that view's frameTimes — exactly the sources described.

7-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `output` *Tongue velocity*?
7-b.decision_correctness_justification: Step for step this reproduces findPosition.m/findVelocity.m: no smoothing for the tongue, interp1 of raw x/y onto the bin centres, np.gradient, NaN velocities set to 0 ('set tongue velocity to 0 if not visible'), and the visibility mask re-imposed afterwards so untracked bins can take class 2. That fidelity is a strength. The problem is the interaction the AI itself discovered and then rationalised: because a visible sample next to an invisible one gets a NaN gradient that is zeroed, and tongue-visible runs are short at 10 ms sampling, a large fraction of visible samples are exactly 0 — the session median is 0.0 in 6 of 12 sessions and ~0.02 in a seventh. The consequence is that those sessions have an empty 'below threshold' class and zero-velocity visible bins are labelled 'above threshold', which inverts the semantics of the output. The AI documented this ('mathematically required by < median versus >= median, not a conversion error') but did not fix it; the reference avoids it by smoothing and differentiating against real frame times within each run of valid frames, which produces no mass at zero. Not wrong given the reference code it follows, but a human should check it.
7-b.code_correctness_justification: velocity_from_xy implements the described steps in the stated order (no fill for the tongue, gradient, non-finite -> 0, hypot, re-mask invisible), and the stored per-session tongue medians (0.0 for JGR2 x2 and JEB19 x4) are consistent with that computation. Units are pixels per 10 ms sample rather than per second, which the metadata states and which does not affect percentile discretisation.

7-c.question: How is `output` *Tongue velocity* thresholded into categories?
7-c.decision_correctness_justification: Per-session 50th percentile of the finite (visible) samples over retained trials and the whole window, with '<' -> 0, '>=' -> 1 and untracked -> 2 — exactly the spec and exactly what the reference does with np.nanpercentile(tongue, 50). The tie convention (equality to the high class) is the literal reading of '< 50th' vs '>= 50th'. The degenerate empty class-0 in half the sessions is inherited from the velocity computation graded in 7-b, not from this rule.
7-c.code_correctness_justification: discretize_session computes np.nanpercentile(subset, 50) on the retained-trial subset and assigns 0/1/2 as described, with an all-class-2 fallback when nothing is finite; the verification log's per-session class fractions match the stored thresholds.

7-d.question: How is `output` *Tongue velocity* aligned with the neural data?
7-d.decision_correctness_justification: Same as the reference: one session-wide video offset computed exactly as findVideoOffset.m (mode(sglx.bitcode.bitstart)/fs - mode(bp.ev.bitStart)), subtracted from frameTimes along with the trial's goCue, and the result placed on the shared bin-centre grid. Computing the offset once per session is the right scope. The realised offsets (0.490 s for 8 sessions, 0.990 s for the 4 JEB19 sessions) are consistent per animal, and the AI checked alignment visually (tongue appears only after the go cue).
7-d.code_correctness_justification: matlab_mode reproduces MATLAB's mode, and `aligned_ft = side_ft - vidshift - go[trial]` is used as the interp1 source axis. The AI's independent raw-source check reproduced the motion-energy categories (same offset machinery) for a whole trial, and the stored vidshift values are recorded in session_info.

8-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `output` *Paw velocity* derived from?
8-a.decision_correctness_justification: The AI uses both bottom-view paw markers (top_paw and bottom_paw) and averages their speeds where available, while the reference uses top_paw alone on the grounds that bottom_paw drops out during the delay epoch. Both appear in the reference params.traj_features, and in the AI's 12 sessions tracking failure is rare (1.4% of frames for top_paw, 2.8% for bottom_paw in the session I checked, 1.6% class-2 bins overall), so averaging is not obviously worse; it is also marker-name agnostic, as the AI argues. Since the two markers are different forepaws rather than two views of one, averaging their speeds is a slightly odd quantity, but it is defensible and symmetric.
8-a.code_correctness_justification: paw_indices is built from whichever of ('top_paw','bottom_paw') are present, raising if neither is, and the per-marker speeds are averaged over the available ones with np.divide(..., where=count>0) leaving NaN when neither is visible — exactly the described behaviour.

8-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `output` *Paw velocity*?
8-b.decision_correctness_justification: Same conceptual pipeline as the reference (clock-correct, resample, differentiate position, take speed magnitude, no cross-view normalisation since only one camera is involved), and more literally faithful to findPosition.m/findVelocity.m in that it applies the reference's nearest-fill for non-tongue features and even reproduces the reference's quirky subtraction of basederiv(1) (the x-component) from both gradients, which it flags in a comment. Crucially it keeps the pre-fill mask so filled samples do not masquerade as tracked data. The resulting distribution (0.492/0.492/0.016) is well behaved.
8-b.code_correctness_justification: velocity_from_xy's non-tongue branch does fill_nearest -> gradient -> subtract baseline_x from both -> hypot -> re-mask, matching the description including the deliberate MATLAB quirk; fill_nearest implements a correct nearest-valid-sample fill.

8-c.question: How is `output` *Paw velocity* thresholded into categories?
8-c.decision_correctness_justification: The same per-session median split with ties to the high class and untracked -> 2 that the reference uses and that the spec mandates; thresholds are computed over retained trials only, as in the reference. The realised per-session fractions are essentially 0.495/0.495/0.01, i.e. a genuine median split with no degeneracy.
8-c.code_correctness_justification: The same discretize_session call is applied to the paw array, and the stored per-session paw medians (0.246-0.675) together with the near-exact 50/50 class split confirm it behaves as described.

8-d.question: How is `output` *Paw velocity* aligned with the neural data?
8-d.decision_correctness_justification: Identical to the reference: the same session video offset and the trial's go cue are subtracted, and the bottom camera's own frameTimes are used because the two views can differ in frame count — the same reasoning the reference gives for timing each feature by its own camera.
8-d.code_correctness_justification: `aligned_ft = bottom_ft - vidshift - go[trial]` is computed from load_trial_traj(f, bottom, trial), independently of the side view's frame times, and is the interpolation source for both paw markers.

9-a.question: What variables in the raw data is `output` *Motion energy* derived from?
9-a.decision_correctness_justification: The standalone motionEnergy_<anm>_<date>.mat file's me.data (one 400 Hz trace per trial), the same source the reference prefers over the sometimes-present obj.me, with the file's manual moveThresh deliberately ignored. The AI unwraps the me.data.data nesting that loadMotionEnergy.m also guards against.
9-a.code_correctness_justification: load_motion_file reads me['data'], unwraps one nested level and returns one array (or None) per trial. Less robust than the reference's while-loop for layouts outside this cohort (a bare cell array with no 'data' field would KeyError), but I confirmed all 12 selected sessions store {data, moveThresh}, so the code works for the cohort it declares.

9-b.question: What processing is involved in computing `output` *Motion energy*?
9-b.decision_correctness_justification: None beyond resampling onto the shared time axis, matching the reference's reasoning that the 99th-percentile-across-pixels reduction has already been done upstream so nothing should be re-derived. The one deviation from loadMotionEnergy.m is that leading-edge NaNs are not nearest-filled but left as the 'no video' class, which is the more honest choice given the spec provides that class and affects only 0.7% of bins.
9-b.code_correctness_justification: The trace is passed straight to interp_matlab with no other transformation and then to discretize_session; the AI's independent check recomputed the whole 500-bin categorical trace for one trial from the raw file and matched, with the threshold agreeing to 1e-12.

9-c.question: How is `output` *Motion energy* thresholded into categories?
9-c.decision_correctness_justification: Per-session 50th percentile over finite samples of retained trials, ties to the high class, missing -> 2, exactly as the reference and the spec require. The AI explicitly considered and rejected the authors' manual bimodal moveThresh because the decoder spec mandates the median, and documented that reasoning — the same trade-off the reference makes implicitly.
9-c.code_correctness_justification: Same discretize_session applied to the motion array; stored thresholds (7.5-19.4 a.u.) and the resulting 0.495/0.497/0.007 split are consistent with a median cut.

9-d.question: How is `output` *Motion energy* aligned with the neural data?
9-d.decision_correctness_justification: Motion energy is timed by the side camera's frameTimes corrected by the session video offset and the trial's go cue, then resampled onto the shared grid — exactly the reference's choice and exactly loadMotionEnergy.m. The AI additionally reproduces that function's catch branch (synthetic 400 Hz axis shifted by 0.5 s) for trials whose frame times are unusable, which the reference solution does not implement.
9-d.code_correctness_justification: The code uses side_ft for the motion-energy interpolation with a comment naming the reference behaviour, and falls back to arange(1,n+1)/400 - 0.5 - go[trial] otherwise; the independent raw-source check reproduced the aligned, binned and discretised trace exactly.

10.question: How are minor mistakes in the data, e.g. missing data, handled?
10.decision_correctness_justification: The same philosophy as the reference — keep the trial and mark the gap rather than invent data. Trials with NaN NdroppedFrames, empty ts, or missing/all-NaN frameTimes are skipped per camera and come out as 500 'not visible' bins; mismatched frameTimes/ts/motion lengths are truncated to the shorter; a non-monotonic time base yields all-NaN rather than garbage; missing motion-energy trials become class 2; spikes with non-finite times or out-of-range trial numbers are dropped. Nearest-filling is applied only where the reference code applies it (non-tongue features) and never overrides the visibility mask. The AI goes beyond the reference in also validating bp array lengths, one-hot outcome/side flags, and finiteness of the converted neural data with explicit raises.
10.code_correctness_justification: Each guard named in the decision exists in the code (load_trial_traj's three early returns, interp_matlab's length truncation and monotonicity test, load_motion_file's None entries, bin_one_unit's valid masks, the Ntrials length checks and the non-finite neural raise), and the full conversion completed without any trial being silently dropped — 3,116 retained trials match the independent count from the raw flags.

11-a.question: What are the most time-consuming steps of the code?
11-a.decision_correctness_justification: Like the reference, the AI concludes that reading the MATLAB files dominates and that the arithmetic afterwards is cheap, and it prints per-session timings to show this. My own profiling of its code confirms the diagnosis and sharpens it: on JEB6, load_behavior_streams (the per-trial HDF5 reads of ts/frameTimes plus interpolation) takes 2.24 s of the 2.53 s session total versus 0.25 s for all neural binning and smoothing. The AI did not name the video loop specifically, but the conclusion (I/O bound, irreducible without changing what is read) is the same as the reference's, and at 27.9 s total for the full run no further optimisation was warranted.
11-a.code_correctness_justification: The timing instrumentation it describes exists (per-session perf_counter, printed per session and stored in session_info as conversion_seconds, plus a total), and the reported 27.91 s matches the logged run.

11-b.question: What loops in the code could have been vectorized to improve efficiency?
11-b.decision_correctness_justification: Like the reference, the AI vectorised the one loop that genuinely could be — spike binning, done in a single np.add.at over all spikes and all trials of a unit — and additionally vectorised the smoothing across all trials at once (the reference smooths per cluster with a single gaussian_filter1d call over the trial-by-time matrix, equivalently). The loops that remain (clusters, trials for the two camera views, trials for output packing) are over ragged per-trial frame counts and are not straightforwardly vectorisable, exactly as the reference argues. The one avenue neither takes is parallelising across sessions.
11-b.code_correctness_justification: bin_one_unit uses searchsorted + np.add.at across all trials, and smooth_reference convolves the whole (n_trials, 515) matrix via sliding_window_view + einsum; the remaining loops are as described.

11-c.question: What processing does the code repeat multiple times?
11-c.decision_correctness_justification: Essentially nothing is recomputed, matching the reference: each file is opened once, the video offset is computed once per session rather than per trial (as findVideoOffset would be called per feature in the MATLAB code), feature-name lists are resolved once per view, the bin grid and smoothing kernel are module-level constants shared by every trial and stream, and each session threshold is computed once. The only repeats I found are trivial: the side-camera aligned frame times are recomputed for motion energy inside the same loop iteration that already computed them for the tongue, and velocity_from_xy rebuilds a visibility mask the caller discards.
11-c.code_correctness_justification: vidshift is computed once in process_session and passed down; KERNEL, TIME and EDGES are module-level; discretize_session is called once per stream. The two small repeats are visible in load_behavior_streams and are arithmetic on a 500-element vector, negligible against the HDF5 reads around them.

11-d.question: What unnecessary processing does the code do that is discarded in downstream analyses?
11-d.decision_correctness_justification: The reference's only waste is in reading fields it never uses; the AI's code has somewhat more: it bins and smooths every unit over all native trials and computes tongue/paw/motion velocities for every native trial before discarding the 14% of trials removed by the early-lick/photostim filter, and it smooths all 528 quality-passing clusters before the >1 Hz cut rejects 10. Smaller items: the visibility mask returned by velocity_from_xy is dropped at every call site, and the per-unit quality counters exist only for metadata. None of this was identified in CONVERSION_NOTES. It is a real but small inefficiency on a 28 s run, and processing all trials first is arguably simpler and less error-prone than threading the retained-trial mask through every stage, so this is a reasonable engineering trade-off rather than a defect.
11-d.code_correctness_justification: The code does what the AI claims it does — no unnecessary file I/O, no redundant loading — and the wasted work I identified is a consequence of processing all native trials before applying `retained`, which is consistent with (rather than contradictory to) its stated design.
